Start here: know where your command will land
Before you create, alter or drop anything, answer four questions from the database itself:
Which database am I connected to? Which role am I using? Which schema is first in
my search path? Which exact object does an unqualified name resolve to?
Picture PostgreSQL as a building. The PostgreSQL server/cluster is the building. A database is a
locked office inside it: one normal connection works inside one database. A schema is a labelled
cabinet inside that office. Two cabinets can both contain a file called orders; the full names
sales.orders and staging.orders keep them distinct.
search_path is a convenience rule that says which cabinets PostgreSQL looks in first when you
write only orders. Convenience becomes risk when two schemas contain the same object
name.
Follow the connection proof with me
Run this only in your learner-owned database:
SELECT current_database() AS database_name,
current_user       AS login_role,
current_schema()   AS current_schema,
current_schemas(true) AS effective_search_path;
SHOW search_path;
SELECT version();
Do not merely save a screenshot. Read the result. If your intended practice database is
standalone_de but current_database() returns postgres, stop. A perfect DROP TABLE against
the wrong database is still a serious mistake.
Create a qualified learner object:
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS m07_lab;
CREATE TABLE m07_lab.connection_check (observed_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
note text NOT NULL);
Now compare:
SELECT to_regclass('connection_check') AS unqualified,
to_regclass('m07_lab.connection_check') AS qualified;
to_regclass is useful while learning because a missing relation returns NULL instead of raising
the same error a direct query would.
Make the search-path risk visible
Create another sandbox schema and deliberately reuse the same table name:
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS m07_retry;
CREATE TABLE m07_retry.connection_check(note text NOT NULL);
SET search_path TO m07_retry, m07_lab, PUBLIC;
SELECT current_schema();
SELECT to_regclass('connection_check');
Before running the last line, predict the result. Then explicitly query
m07_lab.connection_check and m07_retry.connection_check. The lesson is not that
search_path is bad; it is that important cross-schema pipeline SQL should not accidentally
depend on a session setting nobody noticed.
A second beginner trap: client tree versus active session
In pgAdmin you can click one database in the browser tree and still have an older Query Tool tab
connected elsewhere. Trust the active session evidence, not your memory of what you clicked.
In psql, the prompt and \conninfo can help, but the SQL checks above are portable proof.
Your independent proof
Open a fresh connection. Capture database, role, current schema and effective search path
before DDL. Create m07_student plus one qualified table. Close and reopen your client and
prove the object persisted in the intended database/schema.
Then create a second schema with the same table name, alter search_path temporarily, and
write one sentence explaining why schema.table removes ambiguity.
Validate and teach it back
A strong answer is not "schema is like database." Explain the hierarchy accurately: a PostgreSQL
server can host several databases; a connection is normally to one database; schemas are
namespaces inside that database; tables live inside schemas. State one real failure this
distinction prevents.
Changed retry
Use two schemas named raw and serving, each with daily_orders. Predict three resolutions
under three search paths, then verify. Restore the original search path after the exercise. Save
the prediction before the query result.
One more scenario: the query is correct but the object is wrong
Imagine a pipeline creates daily_orders in schema staging for raw ingestion and another
daily_orders in serving for a cleaned consumer table. A developer opens a new session
whose search path starts with serving and runs TRUNCATE daily_orders while believing they
are clearing staging. PostgreSQL did exactly what the session requested. The failure was
context discipline.
A defensive workflow before any destructive DDL/DML is: print the current database; print the
current role; qualify the target schema; count or inspect the target object; then change it. For
example:
SELECT current_database(), current_user;
SELECT count(*) FROM staging.daily_orders;
-- only then, if the learner exercise explicitly requires it:
TRUNCATE staging.daily_orders;
The point is not to add ceremony to every SELECT. The point is to slow down before operations
whose blast radius is large.
Also remember that temporary tables can temporarily change name resolution because
PostgreSQL places a temporary schema early in effective lookup. You do not need to master
temporary-schema internals here; simply notice that an unqualified object name is a request for
PostgreSQL to resolve a name according to session rules. A schema-qualified name tells it
exactly which namespace you mean.
Interview transfer: if someone asks why a query works in one session and fails or points
somewhere unexpected in another, mention database connection, schema/search path,
permissions and object qualification before blaming SQL syntax.
Evidence before you move on
Database/user/schema/search-path capture + same-name schema resolution test. Keep the
genuine first attempt/result/error. A correction made while review is open is repair evidence, not
independent mastery.
Ready-made revision
Without opening the lesson, explain Verify PostgreSQL connection and database/schema
context in 60-120 seconds. State the row/object grain, one realistic failure, one
database-enforced rule (if applicable), and one independent validation. Then reconstruct one
small example from memory.
Protected changed retry
Use raw/serving schemas with the same table name; predict three search_path resolutions
before querying.

Visual/source: freeCodeCamp - Learn PostgreSQL Tutorial - Full Course for Beginners URL:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qw--VYLpxG4 Assigned scope: 41:37-55:55 - CREATE
TABLE, columns and constraints Current reference: PostgreSQL 18 - CREATE TABLE
Reference URL: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-createtable.html Study rule:
Watch/read only the assigned idea, return to this book, type the guided work yourself, then
close video/review/AI solving before the independent attempt.
DDL is a contract, not decoration
When you write CREATE TABLE, you are deciding what future writers are allowed to store. The
safest type is not the type that accepts the most data; it is the type that expresses the meaning
you intend to protect.
Consider four values that all look numeric on screen:
• 0007 is a warehouse code. Adding 2 to it is meaningless, and losing the leading zeros changes
identity. Store it as text.
• 7 cartons is a count. Whole-number arithmetic is meaningful. Store it as an integer.
• 125.50 rupees is an exact business amount. Use exact decimal semantics such as
numeric(12,2) rather than treating money as approximate binary floating point.
• 2026-04-01 is a calendar date. Store a date, not a string you later slice.
That decision is data modeling already.
Follow one table definition slowly
CREATE TABLE m07_student.products (
product_sk bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
product_id text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
product_name text NOT NULL,
category text NOT NULL,
unit_price numeric(12,2) NOT NULL CHECK (unit_price >= 0),
active boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT true,
created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
Read every line as a promise. product_sk is an internal row identity generated by the database.
product_id remains a separate business identifier. numeric(12,2) means at most 12 total
decimal digits with 2 after the decimal point. DEFAULT true is used when the INSERT omits
active; it does not magically turn an explicitly supplied NULL into true when the column is also
NOT NULL.
Date versus timestamp versus timestamptz
Use date for a day such as an invoice date when time-of-day is not part of the fact. Use a
timestamp when you truly have a time. For event instants exchanged across systems,
timestamptz is usually the safer concept because PostgreSQL stores an instant and displays it
in the session timezone. Do not turn this into a timezone deep-dive yet; the habit here is to ask
whether the source means a day or an instant.
DDL that runs can still be wrong
This table will run:
CREATE TABLE bad_example (
order_id integer,
order_date text,
amount text
But it has thrown away three contracts. order_id may lose leading-zero identity; text dates can
contain tomorrow; text amount cannot be reliably aggregated without parsing. Successful DDL
only proves syntax, not design.
Likewise, an aggressive default can invent business data. If a source omits region, DEFAULT
'East' may turn "unknown" into a false fact. Defaults are appropriate only when omission
genuinely has a defined meaning.
Inspect what PostgreSQL actually created
Do not trust only the SQL file you intended to run. Query the catalog:
SELECT column_name, data_type, is_nullable, column_default,
numeric_precision, numeric_scale
FROM information_schema.columns
WHERE table_schema='m07_student'
AND table_name='products'
ORDER BY ordinal_position;
In psql, \d m07_student.products is also useful, but it is a client meta-command rather than
portable SQL.
Your independent design
Create warehouses, shipments, and shipment_lines. Before DDL, write the grain of each table
in plain English. Preserve a code such as 0007 as text. Use one generated surrogate key but
keep a separate unique business key. Choose exact types for quantity, amount, calendar dates
and event timestamps.
Insert one valid row and at least two boundary cases: one that should succeed and one that
should be rejected by type/constraint rules. Save the observed database behavior.
Changed retry
Design receipt headers and receipt lines. The source calls a receipt 000023. Explain why
converting that business key to integer is a semantic change even though PostgreSQL can
numerically store 23.
Work through three type decisions instead of memorizing a type list
Case 1 - money. numeric(12,2) gives you an exact decimal contract for the course's
rupee-like amounts. That does not mean every financial system must use exactly (12,2);
choose precision/scale from realistic maximums and smallest units. A value too large for the
declared precision should fail rather than silently widening the contract.
Case 2 - identifiers. Suppose warehouse_code is 0007. If you store it as integer 7 and later
format it back as four digits, you have created a formatting convention that was not the original
identity. If the business can ever introduce A007, the numeric model breaks completely. Store
identifiers according to identity semantics, not arithmetic appearance.
Case 3 - missing versus default. If active is omitted and the contract truly means new
products start active, DEFAULT true is sensible. If region is absent in the source, defaulting it to
East is inventing a fact. Missingness should remain visible until a business rule justifies a value.
When you review DDL, ask four questions per column: What does this value mean? What
operations are valid? Can it be absent? Who is allowed to invent a default? That checklist is
more transferable than memorizing PostgreSQL type names.
Evidence before you move on
Typed DDL with written grain and catalog inspection, including one meaningful boundary test.
Keep the genuine first attempt/result/error. A correction made while review is open is repair
evidence, not independent mastery.
Ready-made revision
Without opening the lesson, explain Tables, data types and explicit DDL in 60-120 seconds.
State the row/object grain, one realistic failure, one database-enforced rule (if applicable), and
one independent validation. Then reconstruct one small example from memory.
Protected changed retry
Design receipt header/line DDL with leading-zero business ID, exact money, date and one
generated surrogate.

3:16:41-3:25:04 - keys, UNIQUE/CHECK and foreign keys Current reference: PostgreSQL 18 -
CREATE TABLE constraints Reference URL:
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-createtable.html Study rule: Watch/read only the
assigned idea, return to this book, type the guided work yourself, then close video/review/AI
solving before the independent attempt.
Constraints are database-level guardrails
Application code can validate input, but a database may receive writes from Python, SQL clients,
ETL jobs, admin scripts and future services you have never seen. A well-chosen constraint
protects the invariant no matter which writer arrives.
Start with grain. One order_items row represents one line inside one order. Therefore
line_no=1 is allowed in thousands of orders; it cannot be globally unique. The row identity is the
pair (order_id, line_no).
CREATE TABLE m07_source.order_items (
order_id text NOT NULL
REFERENCES m07_source.orders(order_id),
line_no integer NOT NULL CHECK (line_no > 0),
product_id text NOT NULL
REFERENCES m07_source.products(product_id),
quantity integer NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
unit_price numeric(12,2) NOT NULL CHECK (unit_price >= 0),
CONSTRAINT pk_order_items PRIMARY KEY(order_id, line_no)
Naming important constraints makes production errors easier to interpret.
What each rule proves - and what it does not
PRIMARY KEY: this row identity is unique and non-null. It does not prove other business fields
are correct.
FOREIGN KEY: a referenced parent key exists. It does not prove the parent is active, belongs to
the right company, or is the historically correct version for the event date.
UNIQUE: a value or tuple may occur only once under PostgreSQL's uniqueness semantics. It is
useful for business keys, but an SCD2 table intentionally needs several rows for one business
customer, so UNIQUE(customer_id) would be the wrong rule there.
NOT NULL: absence is forbidden. Empty text '' is not NULL, so required meaningful text may
also need a CHECK such as btrim(name) <> ''.
CHECK: a row-level expression must not be false. One subtle point: a CHECK expression
evaluating to NULL does not reject the row. If you need a value to exist and meet a range,
combine NOT NULL with CHECK.
Prove failures inside a safe transaction
Run one test at a time in your sandbox:
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO m07_source.order_items
(order_id,line_no,product_id,quantity,unit_price)
ROLLBACK;
The quantity CHECK should reject it. In PostgreSQL, once a statement errors inside an explicit
transaction, the transaction is typically marked aborted until ROLLBACK (or rollback to a
savepoint). Observe this rather than clicking randomly until the error disappears.
Try four deliberate failures: duplicate composite key, missing parent order, zero quantity and
blank required text in a table that forbids it. Preserve the error messages. Those errors are
successful test evidence.
Do not ask constraints to solve the whole business
Imagine an order references customer C001. The FK can prove C001 exists. It cannot prove the
customer's SCD2 region version was valid on the order date. That is a temporal modeling rule
you will implement later.
Another example: quantity > 0 is easy to enforce per row. "Daily shipped quantity may not
exceed today's warehouse capacity" depends on multiple rows and changing external state; a
simple CHECK is not the right tool.
Your independent proof
Add named constraints to your shipment model. For every constraint, create a two-column note:
1. one bad row this rule catches;
2. one realistic bad state it cannot catch.
That second column is important. It stops you from confusing "database has constraints" with
"data is fully correct."
Changed retry
Build receipt lines with primary key (receipt_id,line_no). Deliberately try PRIMARY
KEY(line_no) in a disposable version and demonstrate why line 1 of receipt R002 collides with
line 1 of R001 even though both are legitimate business rows.
Constraint design also includes deletion behavior
Foreign keys can define actions such as ON DELETE RESTRICT/NO ACTION, CASCADE, SET NULL
and others. Do not choose CASCADE because it makes test cleanup easy. If deleting one
customer should not silently erase historical orders, cascading from customer to order is
probably a dangerous business rule.
For a learner model, the safest default is to make deletion behavior explicit in your reasoning.
Ask: if a parent disappears, should child rows be forbidden, deleted, detached, or retained
through a different archival process? The database cannot choose the business meaning for
you.
Another subtle rule is uniqueness with NULL. Depending on your model and PostgreSQL options,
nullable unique fields require thought: "at most one row with this business value" and "every
row must have a business value" are two separate contracts. UNIQUE and NOT NULL often work
together.
Finally, test the constraint name in the error message. Named constraints such as
ck_order_item_quantity_positive communicate more than autogenerated names when a
pipeline fails at 2 AM. Good names become operational documentation.
Mini transfer: write one sentence explaining why FOREIGN KEY(customer_id) is excellent at
preventing an order for a nonexistent customer, yet useless for proving that the customer's
historical region version matches the order date.
Evidence before you move on
Named PK/FK/UNIQUE/CHECK/NOT NULL failure evidence and constraint-boundary explanation.
Keep the genuine first attempt/result/error. A correction made while review is open is repair
evidence, not independent mastery.
Ready-made revision
Without opening the lesson, explain Primary keys, foreign keys and constraints in 60-120
seconds. State the row/object grain, one realistic failure, one database-enforced rule (if
applicable), and one independent validation. Then reconstruct one small example from memory.
Protected changed retry
Receipt line composite key plus missing-parent/blank-text failure set; state what each rule still
cannot prove.

CONFLICT and UPSERT Current reference: PostgreSQL 18 - INSERT / ON CONFLICT Reference
URL: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-insert.html Study rule: Watch/read only the
assigned idea, return to this book, type the guided work yourself, then close video/review/AI
solving before the independent attempt.
Transactions protect units of work
A data pipeline often performs several related writes. If statement 1 succeeds, statement 2 fails,
and statement 3 never runs, leaving statement 1 permanently committed can create a half-built
state. A transaction gives you an all-or-nothing boundary when you use that boundary
deliberately.
Think of three observable moments: before, inside, after.
SELECT product_id, unit_price
FROM m07_source.products
WHERE product_id='P01';                 -- before: 120.00
BEGIN;
UPDATE m07_source.products
SET unit_price=130
WHERE product_id='P01';
SELECT product_id, unit_price
FROM m07_source.products
WHERE product_id='P01';                 -- inside: 130.00
ROLLBACK;
SELECT product_id, unit_price
FROM m07_source.products
WHERE product_id='P01';                 -- after: 120.00 again
The proof is not that your script contains the word ROLLBACK. The proof is the state you
observed before/inside/after.
What happens after an error
Inside an explicit PostgreSQL transaction, an error usually aborts the transaction. Later
commands are rejected until rollback (or rollback to an earlier SAVEPOINT). Beginners often
keep issuing commands and think PostgreSQL is broken. Read the first error, not the five
follow-on errors it caused.
A savepoint can isolate a smaller experimental step:
BEGIN;
SAVEPOINT before_test;
-- run a risky learner test
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT before_test;
COMMIT;
You do not need savepoints for every pipeline, but knowing they exist helps you understand
transaction state.
UPSERT: rerun safely only when the conflict key matches the grain
Create a current-state feed:
CREATE TABLE m07_lab.product_feed (
product_id text PRIMARY KEY,
product_name text NOT NULL,
unit_price numeric(12,2) NOT NULL
INSERT INTO m07_lab.product_feed(product_id,product_name,unit_price)
VALUES ('P01','Notebook',125.00)
ON CONFLICT (product_id) DO UPDATE
SET product_name = EXCLUDED.product_name,
unit_price   = EXCLUDED.unit_price;
Run the same statement twice. You should still have one P01 row. The rerun converges because
the table's intended grain is one current row per product business ID.
Now ask the question that separates engineering from memorizing syntax: Would product_id
still be the right conflict target in a price-history table? No. Overwriting the current row
would destroy the historical versions you intended to retain.
Idempotent does not mean harmless
A statement can be repeatable and still repeatedly write the wrong value. Idempotency means
repeated execution reaches the same intended state for the same input; correctness still
depends on the input contract, grain and conflict rule.
Your independent proof
Build one current-state supplier table. Save the state after:
1. first INSERT;
2. changed UPSERT;
3. exact rerun of the changed UPSERT.
Then create a transaction with two related writes where the second intentionally violates a
constraint. Roll back and prove the first write did not remain.
Changed retry
Use a different business key and different changed attribute. Then write two sentences
explaining why the same UPSERT pattern is appropriate for current-state supplier contact data
but inappropriate for SCD2 supplier-risk history.
Auto-commit can hide the transaction boundary from beginners
GUI clients often make ordinary statements convenient by committing automatically when you
are not inside an explicit transaction. That convenience becomes confusing when you expect
ROLLBACK to undo something that was already committed in a previous action. For the learner
lab, run the whole BEGIN ... ROLLBACK block deliberately and observe the same session.
A production pipeline also needs to decide what belongs in one transaction. Putting an entire
multi-hour batch in one giant transaction can have operational costs; committing every
individual row can leave partial state. M07 does not prescribe a universal batch size. The
competency is to identify the consistency boundary: which writes must succeed/fail together
for the database to remain meaningful?
For UPSERT, test more than row count. After an exact rerun, verify the business key remains
unique and the stored values are correct. Then run a changed input under the same key and
prove only the attributes you intend to update are changed. If the source provides an immutable
creation timestamp, blindly assigning every column from EXCLUDED can overwrite something
that should never change.
Engineering sentence: ON CONFLICT is not a deduplication strategy by itself. It is a
deterministic response to a particular declared uniqueness conflict.
Evidence before you move on
Before/inside/after rollback proof + current-state UPSERT exact-rerun proof. Keep the genuine
first attempt/result/error. A correction made while review is open is repair evidence, not
independent mastery.
Ready-made revision
Without opening the lesson, explain Transactions, DML and UPSERT in 60-120 seconds.
State the row/object grain, one realistic failure, one database-enforced rule (if applicable), and
one independent validation. Then reconstruct one small example from memory.
Protected changed retry
Supplier current-state upsert + intentional two-write failure; explain why SCD2 cannot use
overwrite semantics.

optimizations-and-where-to-find-them-a-beginners-guide Assigned scope:
Current reference:
PostgreSQL 18 - EXPLAIN Reference URL: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-explain.html
Study rule: Watch/read only the assigned idea, return to this book, type the guided work
yourself, then close video/review/AI solving before the independent attempt.
OPTIONAL
visual - no verified bounded range; EXPLAIN/index context only.
An index is a trade-off, not a trophy
Indexes can reduce the work needed to locate rows, but they consume storage and must be
maintained as rows change. PostgreSQL's planner is allowed to ignore an index when a
sequential scan is cheaper. Your goal is not to force the words "Index Scan"; your goal is to
explain the query shape and plan evidence honestly.
Read EXPLAIN at beginner depth
Start with:
EXPLAIN
SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date
FROM m07_source.orders
WHERE customer_id='C002';
The six-row teaching table will probably prefer Seq Scan. That is sensible: reading six rows can
cost less than consulting an index and then fetching table pages.
At this stage, learn four ideas:
• scan type - sequential scan, index scan, bitmap scan, etc.;
• estimated rows - how many rows the planner expects;
• cost - planner cost units used to compare alternatives, not milliseconds;
• filter/index condition - which predicate is applied where.
EXPLAIN does not execute an ordinary SELECT. EXPLAIN ANALYZE does execute the statement
and adds actual execution evidence. Do not put ANALYZE in front of a modifying statement just
because a tutorial did; in a learner course, keep it to safe read-only statements unless you fully
understand the consequences.
Build a candidate index from a query pattern
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_date
ON m07_source.orders(customer_id, order_date);
The column order expresses a likely access pattern: first locate a customer, optionally narrow
dates. It is not automatically equivalent to an index designed primarily for date-only searches.
Make the experiment large enough to mean something
A tiny table cannot teach selectivity well. In a disposable schema, generate a larger fixture:
CREATE TABLE m07_lab.order_search AS
SELECT g AS row_id,
'C' || lpad(((g % 1000)+1)::text,4,'0') AS customer_id,
DATE '2026-01-01' + (g % 180) AS order_date,
(g % 5000)::numeric(12,2) AS amount
FROM generate_series(1,50000) AS g;
ANALYZE m07_lab.order_search;
First query a selective customer/date range and save the result count. Capture EXPLAIN
(ANALYZE, BUFFERS) if safe in your local sandbox. Then add an index and compare the same
query and same result count. Performance evidence is invalid if the business query changed.
Now change the distribution: ask for a predicate that returns most rows. Predict that the planner
may prefer a sequential scan because the index no longer avoids much work.
Common bad conclusions
"Index exists, therefore query is faster" - unsupported.
"Seq Scan means my index is broken" - false on small/unselective inputs.
"Index every column" - increases write/storage cost and often creates useless structures.
"Lower estimated cost on a 6-row table proves production speedup" - training evidence is too
small for that claim.
Your independent proof
Choose one query pattern from your own M07 tables. State its predicate, expected selectivity
and candidate index before creating the index. Preserve pre/post plans and query-result
controls. Write one downside of the index.
Changed retry
Build a dataset where 95% of rows share one hub_id, then compare a lookup for the dominant
hub versus a rare hub. Predict the difference before reading the plans.
Selectivity changes the usefulness of the same index
Suppose your 50,000-row fixture has about 50 rows for one customer. A predicate on that
customer is selective: most rows are irrelevant. An index can provide a useful shortcut. Now
suppose 47,500 rows have hub_id='H01'. Looking up H01 returns almost the whole table;
sequential reading may be cheaper.
That is why "column is frequently filtered" is not enough to justify an index. Think about how
many rows the predicate returns, how the table is stored, whether ordering matters, and how
often writes must maintain the index.
For a composite B-tree index (customer_id, order_date), a query constraining customer_id
and then a date range fits the ordering well. A date-only query may not benefit in the same way
because the leading key is not constrained. Do not turn this into a rigid rule that PostgreSQL can
never use later columns - the planner has more strategies - but use leading-column order as
your first design intuition.
When comparing plans, call ANALYZE table_name; after a large learner data change so planner
statistics are refreshed. Otherwise you may be judging a plan based on stale estimates.
Validation rule: plan evidence is secondary to correctness. Before performance comparison,
prove both versions return the same row population and key set.
Evidence before you move on
Pre/post EXPLAIN evidence on a query-shaped index with unchanged result controls. Keep the
genuine first attempt/result/error. A correction made while review is open is repair evidence, not
independent mastery.
Ready-made revision
Without opening the lesson, explain Indexes and EXPLAIN evidence in 60-120 seconds. State
the row/object grain, one realistic failure, one database-enforced rule (if applicable), and one
independent validation. Then reconstruct one small example from memory.
Protected changed retry
Create dominant-vs-rare hub distribution and predict plan/index usefulness for each predicate.

Visual/source: Decomplexify - Learn Database Normalization (1NF, 2NF, 3NF...) URL:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GFQaEYEc8_8 Assigned scope: 0:00-20:29 - why
normalize, 1NF, 2NF and 3NF Current reference: PostgreSQL 18 - table constraints / relational
structure reference Reference URL: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/ddl-constraints.html
Study rule: Watch/read only the assigned idea, return to this book, type the guided work
yourself, then close video/review/AI solving before the independent attempt.
Two workloads, two modeling goals
An operational database supports day-to-day state changes: create an order, update a
customer, add a line, enforce references. An analytical database supports questions across
many events: sales by region/month/product, customer history, trends and reconciliations.
You are not learning "normalized good, star schema good-er." You are learning that a model is
designed for a workload and a truth contract.
Start with a bad flat table
Imagine one row per order line containing: order_id, line_no, order_date, customer_id,
customer_name, customer_region, product_id, product_name, quantity, unit_price.
If C001 has 10,000 historical lines, the current customer name and region are copied thousands
of times. When the customer changes region, which rows should change? If you update every
historical row, you may rewrite history. If you update only some, current-state copies disagree.
The flat table has mixed several kinds of truth at line grain.
Normalization as practical dependency thinking
You do not need a theorem-heavy detour. Use these questions:
1NF practical idea: each field holds one value of the intended domain; repeating groups such
as product1, product2, product3 become separate rows/related tables.
2NF practical idea: in a table whose key has multiple columns, non-key attributes should
describe the whole key. In (order_id,line_no), order_date depends on order_id, not the
whole line key; it naturally belongs in the order header.
3NF practical idea: non-key attributes should not depend on another non-key attribute in a
way that causes repeated update facts. If customer_id -> customer_region, repeating region
on every current order line creates an update anomaly.
The point is not to chant 1NF/2NF/3NF in interviews. The point is to see why customers ->
orders -> order_items gives each current operational fact one authoritative home.
Operational current state still does not solve history
Suppose Asha is East in January and moves South on 1 February. The operational customers
row may correctly show only current region = South. A January report asking "region at order
time" needs historical context. Normalization prevented duplicate current-state copies; it did not
automatically create history.
Why analytics deliberately reshapes data
A dimensional star says: choose a fact grain, store measurable events there, and attach
descriptive dimensions. This can intentionally duplicate/reshape some descriptive information to
make analytical joins consistent and understandable. That is a different goal from OLTP update
design.
For this course:
• operational grain: one customer, one order header, one order line;
• analytical fact grain: one completed order line;
• customer dimension: descriptive customer history;
• product dimension: product description;
• fact: event keys, quantity and line amount.

and changes from East to South, both orders would join to South today. That answers
"customer's current region." It does not answer "region when the order occurred." You need to
label the business question before choosing the model.

to orders avoids repeating the header fact on every line - the practical 2NF idea.

attribute of the current customer. Repeating the region across orders creates a dependency
through another non-key fact. Keeping current customer attributes in customers is the practical

descriptive attributes in dimensions because the analytical workload values consistent slicing
and history. That is not "breaking normalization accidentally"; it is a different designed model.

Grain first, tables second
The most expensive dimensional-model mistakes often start before any SQL: nobody agreed
what one fact row means. If one fact row is an order line, every key and measure must be
interpreted at order-line grain.
Our supplied source has 9 order lines totaling 2,280.00. Order O104 is Cancelled with one
500.00 line. The analytical completed-sales population therefore has:
• 8 fact lines;
• 5 distinct completed orders;
• 1,780.00 line amount.
Those three numbers describe the same filtered population at different summaries. We
will use all three because one can catch errors another misses.

version. dim_product describes the product.

quantity, line_amount.
order_id can remain as a degenerate dimension-like business reference in the fact because

Follow the double-counting trap
O101 has two lines:
• 2 notebooks x 120 = 240
• 3 pens x 20 = 60
Total = 300.
If you store order_total=300 on both line rows, then SUM(order_total) returns 600 for O101.
The value is correct per order but placed at the wrong grain.
The same danger applies to one-time shipping fees, order discounts, customer credit limits and
percentages. Before adding a measure to a fact table, ask: Is this value true once per fact
row? Is it additive across the dimensions I plan to sum over?

A dimension join must resolve to exactly one appropriate dimension row per fact. If your SCD2
join matches two overlapping customer versions, one source fact line can become two
warehouse rows. A fact total may then double. Row/key uniqueness checks are part of
dimensional modeling, not optional QA afterthoughts.

Business identity and warehouse row identity are different jobs
A source may call the business customer C001 for years. A warehouse may need several
historical rows for C001. If every historical row used customer_id as the primary key, you could
store only one version. A surrogate key gives each warehouse version its own row identity.
Picture two labels on a dimension row:
• customer_id='C001' answers which business customer?
• customer_sk=17 answers which warehouse row/version?
The fact stores the surrogate key because a January event must attach to the January-valid
dimension version, not whichever customer row happens to be current today.
Follow the SCD2 key design
CREATE TABLE m07_dw.dim_customer (
customer_sk bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
customer_id text NOT NULL,
customer_name text NOT NULL,
region text NOT NULL,
valid_from date NOT NULL,
valid_to date NOT NULL,
is_current boolean NOT NULL,
CONSTRAINT uq_customer_version UNIQUE(customer_id, valid_from),
CONSTRAINT ck_customer_window CHECK(valid_from < valid_to)
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_customer_one_current
ON m07_dw.dim_customer(customer_id)
WHERE is_current;
The primary key makes each warehouse row unique. (customer_id, valid_from) stops
duplicate versions starting on the same date. The partial unique index allows many old versions
but only one row marked current for each business customer.
Why surrogate keys do not solve duplicates by themselves
Imagine your loader inserts the same current customer twice. PostgreSQL can happily generate
customer_sk=21 and customer_sk=22. Both surrogate values are unique, so the primary key is
satisfied. Business duplication remains unless another business/history rule rejects it.
This is the key interview sentence: surrogate uniqueness is row identity; it is not
business-entity uniqueness.
Referential integrity at warehouse grain
fact_order_line.customer_sk can have a foreign key to dim_customer.customer_sk. This
proves the fact points to an existing dimension version. It still does not prove the version was
temporally valid for order_date; your as-of load logic/validation proves that.
Late-arriving or unknown members
Some warehouses use a declared Unknown dimension row so facts can load when a descriptive
record is missing. That can be a legitimate policy, but it must be explicit. A good
unknown-member process preserves the original missing business key, counts the unresolved
facts, and has a repair path. Silently mapping every bad customer to a real-looking fake row
hides source defects.
Do not copy a magic -1 key pattern merely because tutorials do. If you use a reserved unknown
key, document how identity generation and constraints accommodate it.

C999 to an unrelated existing customer just to satisfy the foreign key.

History is a time-window problem
If Asha was East in January and South from 1 February, a January order should not move to
South when you rerun last month's report. SCD Type 2 keeps separate dimension versions and
joins an event to the version valid at event time.
Use half-open intervals:
The left boundary is inclusive; the right boundary is exclusive. An order exactly on 1 February
belongs only to the South row. Adjacent windows can touch without overlapping.
Build one change transactionally
Assume C001 currently has East with valid_to='9999-12-31' and is_current=true. A
simplified change on 2026-02-01 is:
BEGIN;
UPDATE m07_dw.dim_customer
SET valid_to = DATE '2026-02-01',
is_current = false
WHERE customer_id='C001'
AND is_current=true;
INSERT INTO m07_dw.dim_customer
(customer_id,customer_name,region,valid_from,valid_to,is_current)
VALUES
COMMIT;
The two writes belong together. If the new row fails, you do not want the customer left with no
current version.
The as-of fact join
JOIN m07_dw.dim_customer dc
ON dc.customer_id = o.customer_id
AND o.order_date >= dc.valid_from
AND o.order_date <  dc.valid_to
This should map O101 on 2026-01-05 to East and O102 on 2026-02-10 to South.
Joining facts with dc.is_current=true instead would answer a different question: "what is the
customer's current region now?" Both can be legitimate reports. The defect is using one while
claiming the other.
Three invariants you must prove
1. One current row per business key. The partial unique index can enforce this directly.
2. Every version has a valid window. CHECK(valid_from < valid_to) prevents
zero/negative windows.
3. Windows do not overlap. Basic PK/FK rules do not prove this. In an advanced PostgreSQL
design, exclusion constraints/range types can enforce non-overlap; in this beginner module, you
must at least validate it explicitly.
A simple overlap check for two rows of the same customer is conceptually: window A starts
before B ends and B starts before A ends. Use a self-join or window-function validation to search
for such pairs.
Check the history by business result
For C001:
• O101 should report East and 300.00;
• O102 should report South and 600.00.
If both report South, you joined to current state. If either order appears twice, your history
windows likely overlap or your join condition is incomplete.
SCD1 versus SCD2 is a business decision
If a typo in customer name should simply be corrected everywhere, SCD1 overwrite may be
sufficient. If region/risk/tier at event time matters, SCD2 can be justified. History everywhere is
not maturity; it is extra complexity and storage that must answer a real question.

Write a non-overlap check you can actually run
After loading dimension history, search for overlapping versions:
SELECT a.customer_id,
a.customer_sk AS a_sk, a.valid_from AS a_from, a.valid_to AS a_to,
b.customer_sk AS b_sk, b.valid_from AS b_from, b.valid_to AS b_to
FROM m07_dw.dim_customer a
JOIN m07_dw.dim_customer b
ON a.customer_id = b.customer_id
AND a.customer_sk < b.customer_sk
AND a.valid_from < b.valid_to
AND b.valid_from < a.valid_to;
For well-formed half-open history, this should return zero rows. The a.customer_sk <
b.customer_sk condition prevents comparing each pair twice and avoids comparing a row to
itself.
Then check current-row count:
SELECT customer_id,
count(*) FILTER (WHERE is_current) AS current_rows
FROM m07_dw.dim_customer
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING count(*) FILTER (WHERE is_current) <> 1;
Again, a clean result is zero rows.
Finally, test the boundary date itself. A fact exactly on 2026-02-01 must match South, not both
versions. Boundary tests are valuable because many temporal bugs hide at <= versus <.
If your business stores timestamp-effective changes rather than day-effective changes, the
same half-open idea applies with timestamp/timestamptz values; do not round them to dates
unless the business contract truly works at date grain.

A file crossing into PostgreSQL is a trust boundary
A CSV is text on a filesystem. A governed PostgreSQL target has typed columns, keys and
constraints. Staging is the deliberate boundary between those worlds.
The safe beginner pattern is: landing file -> raw staging -> profile/validate -> accepted
target + rejected/quarantine -> reconciliation.
Do not load a messy vendor file straight into final tables just because COPY is fast.
Server-side COPY versus psql \\copy
This difference causes endless beginner confusion.
COPY m07_stage.customer_raw
FROM '/some/path/customer_stage_bad.csv'
WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER true);
This SQL tells the PostgreSQL server process to read a file path from the server's point of
view. The file must be accessible to that process and server-side file privileges apply.
Inside the psql program:
SET search_path TO m07_stage;
\copy customer_raw(customer_id,customer_name,region,signup_date_text) FROM 'customer_stage_bad.csv' CSV HEADER
\copy is a psql meta-command, not ordinary SQL. The client reads the local file and streams it
through the connection. A laptop path can therefore work with \copy when server-side COPY
FROM '/laptop/path' cannot.
pgAdmin's import/export interface is another client workflow. Always know which
machine/process is expected to open the path.

CREATE TABLE m07_stage.customer_raw (

customer_id text,
customer_name text,
region text,
signup_date_text text

PostgreSQL 18 awareness: COPY can handle some row errors
Current PostgreSQL 18 COPY supports options such as ON_ERROR and REJECT_LIMIT for
supported input-error handling. That is useful current behavior, but it does not replace your
business-quality staging design. A syntactically valid row with a blank region or duplicate
business key can still be business-invalid. Keep the staging/quarantine pattern as the course's
auditable method.
Common failure modes
• File path is interpreted on the wrong machine.
• Header/delimiter/encoding does not match the file.
• Direct typed load stops before raw bad values are inspectable.
• Duplicate detection is performed after a destructive dedupe, losing evidence.
• Counts are compared across different source filters.

Turn reject logic into inspectable SQL
After raw staging, do not immediately DELETE bad rows. Create a diagnostic view/query that
assigns reasons. For example, a beginner-friendly pattern can compute flags such as
blank_region, bad_date_text and duplicate_business_key, then route rows based on those
flags.

A date-shaped string is not necessarily a real date: 2026-02-31 matches a simple YYYY-MM-DD pattern but is invalid. PostgreSQL 18 provides pg_input_is_valid(text, 'date'). Use it with a format check, then cast only in the valid CASE branch. Keep the invalid original text in quarantine. The complete example below uses this approach.
Keep duplicate handling deterministic. In the supplied fixture, the first valid C201 is accepted
and the later duplicate is rejected for this exercise. A real system may use source timestamps,
sequence numbers or a merge policy instead. Never use "drop duplicates, keep first" without
knowing what determines first.
For each run, save a load identifier or file name when possible. Then a reject row answers not
only "why rejected?" but also "from which source run?" This becomes invaluable when the same
business key appears in several files.

A worked validation query

After the five rows are loaded, the following query assigns a single first reason to each row. The valid first C201 is kept; its later duplicate is rejected. Rank is defined by source_row, not arbitrary database display order.
WITH flagged AS
(SELECT *,
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id
ORDER BY source_row) AS key_occurrence
FROM m07_stage.customer_raw), CHECKED AS
(SELECT *,
CASE
WHEN NULLIF(TRIM(region), '') IS NULL THEN 'blank_region'
WHEN signup_date_text !~ '^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$'
OR NOT COALESCE(pg_input_is_valid(signup_date_text,
'date'),
FALSE) THEN 'invalid_date'
WHEN key_occurrence > 1 THEN 'duplicate_customer' ELSE NULL
END AS reject_reason
FROM flagged)
SELECT source_row, customer_id, reject_reason,
CASE
WHEN reject_reason IS NULL THEN signup_date_text::date
END AS accepted_signup_date
FROM CHECKED
ORDER BY source_row;

For this supplied fixture, two rows have a null reject_reason and three have a reason. Keep the raw fields beside the reason when writing your reject table. The query is a demonstration for this fixture, not a universal customer-data contract; add explicit ID/name rules when you define a broader source contract. The official PostgreSQL 18 reference for pg_input_is_valid is https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/functions-info.html .

Least privilege is part of pipeline correctness
A pipeline that "works" only because every connection is superuser has hidden risk. Routine jobs
should receive only the permissions needed for their responsibility.
PostgreSQL uses roles. A role can be allowed to log in, can own objects, can be a member of
other roles, and can receive object privileges. Ownership is powerful: the owner has inherent
control over the object. That is different from granting SELECT or INSERT to a routine role.
Separate responsibilities on paper first
A simple local learning design:
Role
Intended responsibility
m07_owner
own schemas/tables; migration/admin use
m07_ingest
write only required staging/load targets
m07_analyst
read serving/warehouse tables only
This is not a universal production role model. It is a way to learn boundaries.
Schema privileges and table privileges are different
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA m07_dw TO m07_analyst;
GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA m07_dw TO m07_analyst;
USAGE on a schema allows resolving/accessing objects in the namespace; it does not
automatically grant SELECT on the tables. Conversely, table privileges without the necessary
schema access can still leave a role unable to use the object normally.
CREATE on a schema is more powerful: it allows a role to create objects there. Do not grant it
just to silence an error.
Test denials, not only successes
In a safe local instance where you control the roles, test:
• analyst can SELECT m07_dw.fact_order_line;
• analyst cannot INSERT into it;
• analyst cannot read raw staging if staging is intentionally private;
• ingest can write its approved target but cannot alter ownership/admin objects.
A denied operation is valuable evidence when denial is the policy.
You can use a separate login or, where appropriate and permitted, SET ROLE to test effective
privileges. Do not experiment with role creation on a school/work/shared server.
Future objects are a common trap
A grant on all tables that exist today does not automatically mean a table created tomorrow
gets the same grant. ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES can define privileges for future objects
created by a particular owner/role. The "particular owner" detail matters: default privileges are
tied to the role whose future objects are being created.
This is why an access design should include object ownership and creation workflow, not only a
list of GRANT statements.
Secrets and authentication stay outside this lesson
Database roles are authorization inside PostgreSQL. Password storage/secret managers and
network authentication are broader concerns covered later. Never place real company
passwords or credentials into course evidence.
Your independent proof
Create a privilege matrix before SQL. If you own a safe local PostgreSQL instance and have
rights, implement the roles and save successful and denied test statements. If you cannot safely
create roles, label the artifact PLAN-ONLY / NATIVE TEST PENDING. Honest pending
evidence is better than a fake pass.

Read one privilege failure like an engineer
Suppose m07_analyst can resolve m07_dw.fact_order_line and SELECT from it, but an INSERT
fails with permission denied for table fact_order_line. That error is a pass if the policy
says analysts are read-only.
Do not respond by granting ALL PRIVILEGES. Find the operation the role genuinely needs and
grant only that scope. Similarly, granting table SELECT but forgetting schema USAGE can
produce a different access failure; fix the missing layer rather than overprivileging the whole
database.
Ownership should also be deliberate. If your routine ingestion login owns every table, it can
often do much more than its job requires. Many production setups separate migration/object
ownership from runtime roles. M07's small m07_owner / m07_ingest / m07_analyst model is
meant to make that separation visible.
When you document default privileges, state whose future objects the rule applies to. A
common surprise is configuring defaults as one role and later creating tables as another role,
then wondering why the expected grants did not appear.
A strong handoff therefore includes both the privilege matrix and the object-creation/ownership
convention.

Picture the recovery test

The first database remains your source. pg_dump writes a portable logical archive. pg_restore reconstructs a different, empty database from that archive. You then run the same counts, totals, keys and history query on both. The check proves reconstruction; merely opening the archive file proves very little.
Work through the commands

Run the three printed commands in your operating-system terminal, one at a time. First confirm PostgreSQL command-line tools are available and your connection reaches standalone_de. The new target standalone_de_restore_test must be disposable and must not already contain your working tables. If createdb says it already exists, choose a new test database name and use that same name in pg_restore; do not delete your working database to clear the error. A password prompt may be normal for your installation. Keep passwords out of the command text. After restoration, run the supplied control SQL against the restore target and compare with the source: 9 source rows / 2280.00 and 8 completed facts / 1780.00. A mismatch means the recovery task is not complete even if pg_restore exited successfully.

A database handoff is proven by recovery
A SQL file in Git is useful. A .dump file is useful. Neither proves that another clean target can
reconstruct the database and pass the same controls.
Treat schema change and recovery as two connected engineering questions:
1. Can I evolve this database without leaving consumers in an unknown state?
2. Can I rebuild/recover it somewhere else and prove the rebuilt copy is correct?
Use staged schema changes
Suppose a production-like table needs a new required source_system column. A beginner's
instinct is:
ALTER TABLE big_table
ADD COLUMN source_system text NOT NULL;
On a populated table that may fail immediately because existing rows have no value, and some
changes can hold locks or affect old application versions.
A safer conceptual sequence is:
1. add the column nullable or with a deliberately safe transition rule;
2. backfill existing rows in controlled batches/transaction strategy;
3. validate there are no remaining invalid/missing values;
4. update writers/readers;
5. enforce NOT NULL only when the contract is true;
6. keep rollback/repair thinking documented.
The exact production migration strategy depends on size, traffic, locks and application
compatibility. M07 teaches the habit, not universal zero-downtime migration magic.
Understand what pg_dump does
pg_dump makes a logical export of one PostgreSQL database. It can produce plain SQL or
archive formats. It does not, by itself, export cluster-wide roles/tablespaces; those global objects
require separate handling such as pg_dumpall options/administration.
Example local commands for a custom-format dump:
pg_dump -Fc -d standalone_de -f m07.dump
createdb standalone_de_restore_test
pg_restore -d standalone_de_restore_test m07.dump
These are shell commands, not SQL. Connection parameters and authentication vary. Do not
paste passwords into a shared shell history or course file.
The restore target must be different
Restoring back over the same working database does not prove you can reconstruct a clean
environment. Use a separate database such as standalone_de_restore_test (or another
isolated test target you control).
After restore, rerun independent controls:
• expected schemas/tables exist;
• source rows = 9;
• source amount = 2,280.00;
• completed fact rows = 8;
• completed fact amount = 1,780.00;
• C001 historical orders map East then South;
• representative constraints/keys still exist;
• one representative query returns the same business result.
A file-exists check is not a recovery test.
Handoff is more than backup
A second engineer needs:
• ordered setup/migration SQL;
• required PostgreSQL version/extension assumptions;
• load order and source-file contracts;
• role/privilege plan;
• known reconciliation controls;
• backup/restore commands;
• what was actually tested versus still pending;
• which folders are source artifacts versus generated evidence.
Hidden local paths are a common failure. If your restore instructions say
/Users/ashish/Desktop/final2/..., the handoff is not reproducible on another machine.
Your independent proof
Make one additive schema change in the learner DB. Document pre-check, forward steps,
validation and repair/rollback thinking. Create a logical dump and restore it to a second
database if the PostgreSQL command-line tools are available. Run the controls again on the
restore target.
If the tools are unavailable, leave the restore item pending. Do not convert a written plan into
"PASS."

Restore validation should detect more than missing rows
After restoring to a clean target, check several layers:
1. schemas/tables/views/indexes expected by the module exist;
2. key constraints still reject a known invalid row in a rolled-back test;
3. row and amount controls match;
4. the SCD2 as-of report still maps O101 East and O102 South;
5. a representative role/privilege plan can be recreated (remember a single-database pg_dump
does not automatically capture every cluster-global role);
6. the README commands do not depend on your personal absolute path.
Why test constraints after restore? A data-only export can reproduce rows while omitting some
schema objects depending on how the backup was made/restored. Why test the business
report? Object counts can all match while a migration altered logic or history. Recovery
evidence should climb from structure to data to business result.
For a schema migration, capture before/after metadata as well as data. If you add
source_system, prove pre-existing rows were backfilled to the intended value before enforcing
NOT NULL. If an application/pipeline version must coexist during rollout, document that
compatibility assumption instead of pretending the database change is isolated.
This is the beginning of DataOps thinking that will become much more explicit in M16. A
trustworthy handoff lets another engineer reproduce the database without inheriting invisible
assumptions from your laptop, shell history or memory.
